However, he wrote, that was merely a technical error that does not require Belgal to be released from federal custody pending deportation proceedings.

items.title: How a $1B Obama-era solar plant went bankrupt twice, leaving taxpayers with the tab
items.summary:
TONOPAH, Nev. — An Obama-era solar power plant once hailed as a "clean energy marvel" and backed by more than $1 billion in federal support has gone bankrupt for a second time and sold for just $7 million — with the estimated taxpayer tab potentially reaching $507.6 million.

Rising from the barren Nevada desert, the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project looks like a futuristic fortress in a vast, dusty wasteland, with more than 10,000 mirrors surrounding a giant central tower. The plant was designed to generate solar electricity even after sunset, using an emerging technology that promised to revolutionize green energy in America.

The Obama administration bet big on the project, backing it with a $737 million federal loan guarantee and around $275 million in Treasury grant awards as part of its broader $90 billion push to combat climate change and stimulate the economy following the 2008 financial crisis.

OBAMA-ERA 'CLEAN ENERGY' SOLAR POWER PLANT STILL USES FOSSIL FUELS – AND KILLS THOUSANDS OF BIRDS ANNUALLY

But the promise never matched the performance.

After operations began in late 2015, leaks and equipment failures…
items.t: How a $1B Obama-era solar plant went bankrupt twice, leaving taxpayers with the tab

items.title: Trump orders federal contractors to alert White House on congressional record requests
items.summary:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday instructing federal contractors to notify the White House of congressional information requests and withhold material the administration deems privileged, a move that comes as Democrats prepare to launch oversight investigations.

The order applies to all federal contractors and subcontractors. Companies that fail to comply risk losing their existing contracts or being suspended from future work, according to the order.

Trump framed the directive as a pushback against lawmakers whom the order accuses of "harassing private companies" to get confidential executive branch information.

SUPREME COURT URGED TO DEFANG ‘CRIMINAL TRAP’ THAT HAS SENT TRUMP OFFICIALS TO PRISON

The order could invite legal challenges, particularly if contractors are told to withhold records sought by subpoena. Although executive privilege lets presidents protect certain internal communications, courts can intervene in clashes over congressional oversight powers.

The order builds on a directive issued earlier this week by White House Counsel Will Scharf,…
items.t: Trump orders federal contractors to alert White House on congressional record requests

items.title: Republicans face 'brutal' 2028 Senate map after Dems 2026 blue wave
items.summary:
Incoming Senate Republican campaign chairman says the party faces a "very tough" road ahead as the GOP aims to take back their majority in 2028 after taking significant losses in the midterms earlier this month.

Democrats convincingly grabbed control of the Senate and will hold a large 56-44 majority when the new Congress is sworn in at the start of the new year, they also won control of the House and multiple governors' seats flip from red to blue, as well.

In the Senate, the new split means Republicans will need to flip at least six seats in the 2028 elections to win back the majority. That number rises to seven seats if they lose the White House in the next election cycle.

One senator told Fox News Digital that Republicans can "forget 2028."

"It is an absolutely brutal map," Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, the incoming National Republican Senatorial Committee chair, recently told Fox News Digital, as he pointed to the states up for grabs in 2028.

SENATE REPUBLICANS FEAR 'BRUTAL' 2028 MAP COULD KEEP DEMOCRATS IN POWER FOR YEARS

But the first term senator from Ohio added that in "politics, things change pretty quickly."

He's not…

items.title: Millions could lose paid benefits due to Congress ignoring decades of Social Security warnings: experts
items.summary:
A panel filled with top economists, including a Nobel Peace Prize winner, warned Congress decades ago that their reforms to Social Security could spell disaster. 

Now, experts tell Fox News Digital that group from a bygone era was right, as the safety-net program hurtles toward a crisis that could affect millions. 

"Social Security benefits were put on autopilot back in 1977," Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow of the American Enterprise Institute, told Fox News Digital. "Since then, Congress has done as little as it possibly could."

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., unveiled a report on the decades-old program that blasted it as a "Ponzi scheme," and warned that Social Security’s slide into insolvency began in the 1970s, when, despite warnings, lawmakers opted to tie benefit growth to wages rather than inflation.

AMERICANS MISLED ON SOCIAL SECURITY FOR DECADES AS CLOCK COUNTS DOWN ON BENEFITS, EXPLOSIVE REPORT REVEALS

Johnson wrote in his report that at the time, an expert panel was formed that warned lawmakers that if they were to tie benefits to inflation, "Social Security would likely be sustainable today."

Still, lawmakers at the time ran with their own amendments to the program, which were signed into law by former President Jimmy Carter in December 1977.

"What they said in 1977 was if you index benefit growth to wages,…

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson (D) is fighting to keep his name on the 2027 ballot at the exact moment his administration is engulfed in a fiscal and leadership meltdown at City Hall.

Election officials are reviewing challenges to more than 25,000 of Johnson's nominating signatures ahead of the Feb. 23, 2027, mayoral election — a threshold fight unfolding just days after his third chief financial officer in 10 months abruptly resigned, Standard & Poor's placed Chicago's credit rating on negative watch and the City Council voted 45-5 to investigate three years of city financial reporting for possible misstatements.

Despite the mounting pressure, Johnson brushed off questions about whether he will survive the ballot challenge.

"Yeah, feeling just fine, I'm going to be on the ballot," Johnson told ABC 7 Chicago about the challenge. "Looking forward to building the safest, most affordable big city in America, and we're going to continue to do that work."

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan to gut the city’s tactical police unit is not what is seems, two former high-ranking NYPD officials tell Fox News Digital.

They argue the stunt is a political sleight of hand in which specialized officers responsible for handling violent protests will be rebranded under a different name despite the socialist mayor's promise to disband it completely.

"The problem is…day-to-day New Yorkers don't understand all this gas lighting," former NYPD Chief John Chell told Fox News Digital. "And they feel the angst of it."

"But at the end of all that, this is nothing more than smoke and mirrors," he added.

EXCLUSIVE: RETIRED POLICE SERGEANT ISSUES WARNING OVER MAMDANI'S NYPD SHAKE-UP AHEAD OF THANKSGIVING PARADE

The move to dissolve the Strategic Response Group (SRG) and replace it with a "first-of-its-kind" civilian dialogue team fulfills one of Mamdani's campaign promises — noted in the first sentence of his news release on the move.

items.summary:
Kentucky’s top auditor says her office has uncovered $1.5 billion in taxpayer waste across state government and accused Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, widely believed to have presidential aspirations, of brushing off the findings instead of helping fix them.

"I wish I could say that I had more support and help from the governor's office in Kentucky, but I haven't really and that's one of the reasons why I'm very public with our reports. I'm very public with our findings, because I need the public's help," Ball said in an interview this week at a State Financial Officers Foundation (SFOF) conference in Philadelphia.

"I need the backlash that comes when you see money just being flushed down the toilet, when you see that you're losing money, especially in Medicaid. It's money that should go to people who are actually in need, and we're losing those dollars."

Over the past year, Ball’s office flagged $836 million in wasteful Medicaid spending that was primarily driven by multi-state concurrent enrollment, where Kentucky continued paying monthly managed care capitation fees for individuals simultaneously enrolled in Medicaid in up to eight other states.

Ten years ago this month, Stephen Port was convicted of the murders of four young gay men lured to their deaths via the dating app Grindr.

But it took another five years for their families to learn through an inquest what some had long suspected: that the Metropolitan police’s failure to link the murders quickly enough may have contributed to the later deaths, raising difficult questions over whether that would have happened if the victims were straight. The year after that, officers at Charing Cross station were caught WhatsApping each other rape jokes and insults like “fuck you bender”, contributing to Louise Casey’s conclusion in a review not long afterwards that the force was both institutionally homophobic and misogynistic.

In a recent interview with the Texas Tribune, Hinojosa, a Democrat, dismissed Abbott’s January directive restricting new H-1B visa petitions as a distraction.

"Yeah, that does not make sense to me. I will tell you, I’m not doing culture wars. That’s not what I was elected to do," Hinojosa said.

Abbott issued the order in January to bar state agencies and public universities from filing new H-1B petitions without written approval from the Texas Workforce Commission, citing reports that employers had displaced U. S. workers with lower-paid foreign labor.

Fiona the hippo received a formal tribute from the U. S. Senate on Friday, one day after the beloved Cincinnati Zoo resident died following a medical emergency.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, introduced the resolution honoring Fiona's life and legacy while expressing the chamber's gratitude to the zoo's staff for their care and dedication. The measure passed by unanimous consent.

Speaking from the Senate floor next to a photo of the hippopotamus, Moreno described Fiona's death as a "devastating loss" and a tragic accident.

"The people who come to our city, our state, that now don’t have Fiona there," Moreno said. "It’s going to leave a hole in the zoo and a hole in their heart."

The tribute came one day after the Cincinnati Zoo announced that Fiona died after ingesting a knit hat that accidentally landed in her enclosure last week. According to the zoo, a visitor tossed the hat into the air outside the exhibit, where it caught on a ceiling fan and was launched over the viewing windows into her habitat.

items.title: Trump wags finger at 'really rude' reporter, tells her she belongs in the 'back row' during press exchange
items.summary:
President Donald Trump rebuked a female reporter at the end of a White House news conference Friday, wagging his finger at her, calling her "really a rude person" and telling her she belonged in the "back row."

The exchange unfolded as Trump wrapped up a lengthy news conference following his return from an Asia trip, just after inviting White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to the podium and praising Miller's work on immigration and deregulation.

Before addressing the press corps, Trump defended Miller's temperament, noting that critics often view him as overly strict on immigration.

CHINA BLOCKS BLOOMBERG REPORTER FROM TRUMP-PUTIN-XI MEETING OVER QUESTION TO TRUMP

"He’s really a talent, and he’s got a big heart. A lot of people think he doesn’t. They think he’s hard on immigration, harder on this. He’s got a tremendous heart. In many ways. "Who are you with. Who are you with?" Trump asked while waving his finger in her direction.

After the reporter replied, "Who are you?" Trump sharply criticized both her demeanor and her seating placement in the room.

items.title: Andy, António and Ursula: the joyful EU throuple break Nigel’s bitter heart | John Crace
items.summary:
The passionate PM was unafraid to rush in. This could be the start of something lasting … if people could conquer their trust issues

Forget the smell. You could almost taste the madeleines. Those late nights in Brussels from 10 years ago when time had lost all meaning. So it seemed it might be on Friday. A press conference scheduled for 12.30pm pushed back a quarter of an hour. And then another 15 minutes. Yet another 15 minutes. There are few things the EU does better than taking negotiations down to the wire.

But there the similarities ended. Because when the presser eventually started about an hour later than planned, everything was sweetness and light. António Costa, president of the European Council, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Andy Burnham presented themselves as the perfect throuple. It had been love at first sight, and they couldn’t wait for their next tryst. They could barely take their eyes off one another. A far cry from the bad old days of Brexit where Theresa May was left on her own with only four pot plants for company.

Continue reading...

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage

Senior correspondent

Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said.

Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months, a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China.

But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today.

This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state.

It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink.

“We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.”

items.title: Biden memoir draws fire for ‘denial’ as critics flag Gaza, racial-equity omissions
items.summary:
Former President Joe Biden’s new memoir has drawn sharp criticism and opened a debate about how Biden’s choices — and his account of them — will shape his legacy.

Released Nov. 17, "Promise Me, America" defends Biden’s presidency and his decision to seek re-election in 2024. The memoir drew a sharp verdict from The New Yorker writer Amy Davidson Sorkin, who said Biden remains "stubbornly in denial," while other critics scrutinized the book's account of Gaza and what it left out about racial equity. Sorkin’s criticism centers on Biden’s response to questions about his age and his continued insistence that he could have won.

"The true test of a book like this is whether its author will own his losses, too. Biden, for his part, does not," added New York Times nonfiction critic Jennifer Szalai. "He is so preoccupied with burnishing his legacy that he gets awkward and defensive when addressing the two issues many readers will be most curious about: his handling of the war in Gaza, and his decision to run for a second term."

"The news of the memoir, in short, is that there is no real news: Biden is as stubbornly in denial as ever, " Sorkin wrote.

BIDEN ADDRESSES INFAMOUS 'WE BEAT MEDICARE' DEBATE MOMENT IN NEW MEMOIR

The dispute around Biden's recollection of…

The deadlock initiated the unique tiebreaker last week in which each candidate would have the chance to win two of three coin flips.

THREE HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL TEAMS HAVE THEIR PLAYOFF FATES DECIDED BY A MIDNIGHT PARKING LOT COIN TOSS

Under the city's election rules, each candidate had a chance to call the coin's landing. Herrold went first, calling heads, but the coin landed tails, giving Lagner a 1-0 lead.

Lagner went next, accurately predicting heads to win the contest, securing her election victory to become city commissioner.

"This shows how great and free our country is," Lagner told a local news…

items.title: Trump and Dana White honor Marine Corps band with six-figure checks in first event on new helipad
items.summary:
FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump and UFC President and CEO Dana White will announce six-figure personal contributions to one of America's oldest musical institutions.

The President’s Own United States Marine Band played a key role in America's 250th birthday celebrations and official state business this year — and a White House official tells Fox News Digital that the pair want to "express their appreciation for the band’s exceptional talent, professionalism and commitment to excellence."

Trump and White announced Friday afternoon on the new White House helipad on the South Lawn that they increased their combined gift from $200,000 to $500,000 of their own money after realizing the size of the ensemble. No taxpayer dollars will be used for the $500,000 gift.

"Now, it started off with 200,000, and I said, how many people are there? I thought there were 70, but it’s about 107. And a lot of people joined. So we decided to increase it," Trump said during the event, which was the first-ever held on the new South Lawn helipad.

"We’re now making it at 500,000. Now everyone’s going to get a lot of money," Trump added.

All 135 members of the band will attend alongside senior military leaders, including Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and Commandant of the Marine Corps General Eric Smith.

items.title: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins
items.summary:
In other countries, local communities have a say in their futures. If the UK were truly democratic, everywhere would be a parish in control of its own fate

Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections.

And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist, author and BBC broadcaster. His book The Village in Britain: And Why Place Matters is…

items.title: While the headlines rave about Milburn’s Neets review, the young people I know are angry and frustrated | Felicity Halstead
items.summary:
The focus seems to be on welfare reform as a way to deal with youth unemployment. But young people just want a fairer jobs market

  • Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity

I was at my desk last Thursday morning as a steady stream of young people filed into GoodWork’s central London community hub for a day of employability workshops. Despite the accusations of disengagement among young people, they didn’t need me to tell them that proposals to cut some benefits for under-25s were all over the news. I could hear them talking about it as soon as the lift pinged open – and the mood was low.

Alan Milburn has made a concerted effort to say that he doesn’t believe young people are to blame for dire levels of youth unemployment. He says the system has let them down and only a decade-long transformation will fix a problem that is complex and deeply entrenched. Simply recognising the scale of the problem and being willing to invest in a solution is a positive start.

Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity

Germans are not the love-letter writing kind of people. When we write a letter, a complaint is usually not far off. But we cannot complain about you. About other things, yes: transatlantic relations, or Trump, ja, ja. Or our own chancellor, who every morning talks about reforms which, by the evening, we know will never get done. But when I think about Britain I feel only one thing: longing.

items.title: ‘It stings to come close’: Louisiana Democrat’s narrow failure to make it 57 Senate seats
items.summary:
Jamie Davis falls just short as Democrats across south wonder whether blue wave could have been even bigger

Democrats are celebrating after, with Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska, they have officially secured 56 Senate seats after the midterm elections. But Jamie Davis, who lost an incredibly close election for a Senate seat in Louisiana and could have made it 57, told the Guardian it “stings to come close”.

In Louisiana, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, Davis lost to the Republican congresswoman Julia Letlow 49.1% to 50.9%. He was about 25,000 votes short in a state that cast about 1.5m votes.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘It stings to come close’: Louisiana Democrat’s narrow failure to make it 57 Senate seats

items.title: The ‘blue wave’ could foil the Trump administration’s Big Bend wall plans
items.summary:
Supreme court greenlit federal government’s plan to rampage through national park, but with Texas now flipped, there will be more hurdles

The Trump administration’s plans to build a “smart border wall” through a 500-mile stretch of Texas that includes the Big Bend national park recently got the green light from the supreme court. But those efforts are likely to slam into a big, blue wall.

Last week’s decision – the result of a continuing challenge to the administration’s decision to waive dozens of federal laws to speed wall construction in the Big Bend region – dealt a major blow to environmentalists and park enthusiasts, as well as locals who value the region’s remoteness, landowners who could see their properties devalued and businesses that rely on outdoor tourism.

Continue reading...
items.t: The ‘blue wave’ could foil the Trump administration’s Big Bend wall plans

items.title: After a blue wave, Trump will dig in his heels. We must be more vigilant than ever | Steve Cohen and Michael Shank
items.summary:
Anti-democratic behaviors won’t disappear overnight. The new Congress – and all of us – must rise to the occasion

Americans just witnessed a blue tsunami in the midterm elections, with historic firsts across many US states: the country’s first female Black governor, first female Native American governor, first Muslim US senator, and more.

And while the voters’ repudiation of Donald Trump’s agenda is clear, as Democrats seize the majority of both chambers of Congress, the work to defend our institutions from further democratic backsliding won’t ease up overnight.

Continue reading...
items.t: After a blue wave, Trump will dig in his heels. We must be more vigilant than ever | Steve Cohen and Michael Shank
